title: Chase Software Bug Ripples Across US Banks, Stalling Zelle Payments for Hours
excerpt: A fault in JPMorgan Chase's own systems delayed transactions nationwide on Monday, surfacing as errors at Wells Fargo, Bank of America and other banks whenever a Zelle payment touched Chase. Chase said it was fixed by Monday evening.
body:
• A software bug at JPMorgan Chase on Monday, November 16 slowed transactions for hours and rippled to customers of Wells Fargo, Bank of America, U.S. Bank, Capital One and Truist, largely through Zelle payments between banks.
  • Chase outage reports on Downdetector peaked at about 4,800 around 2 p.m. ET; Chase said the issue was resolved by about 7 p.m. ET and that "transactions are being processed normally now."
  • Chase said the fault was a technical issue in its own systems, not a cyberattack; Bank of America and U.S. Bank said their own systems were not directly hit - delays appeared when a payment involved Chase on the other side.
  • What it means for you: if a Zelle payment to or from a Chase account stalled on Monday, it should now go through; Bank of America advised customers seeing delays with other providers to contact those providers directly.

A software bug inside JPMorgan Chase slowed bank transactions across the United States for much of Monday, November 16, delaying payments for customers of several of the country's largest banks before Chase declared the problem fixed in the evening. JPMorgan Chase confirmed to USA Today that the problems stemmed from Chase.

The fault sat in Chase's on-premises systems, according to Livemint's report, and spread mainly through Zelle, the bank-owned payments network. When a customer of another bank sent or received a Zelle payment involving a Chase account, the transaction stalled and error messages surfaced on both banks' services - which is why outage reports spiked at Wells Fargo, Bank of America, U.S. Bank, Capital One and Truist even though the fault was Chase's.

"ET the bank told USA Today the issue had been resolved and was related to a "software bug"; by 7:25 p.m."

How the day unfolded

Zelle problem reports began around 9:30 a.m. ET and climbed through the afternoon. On Downdetector, Chase reports reached about 4,800 around 2 p.m. ET, the highest of any bank. Luke Kehoe, lead industry analyst at Downdetector's parent company Ookla, told USA Today that Chase recorded its second-highest volume of outage reports in a 15-minute window in at least a year. Of the Chase problems reported, about 53% concerned account balances and transactions, 20% were login issues and 17% involved transfers, according to the Downdetector breakdown cited by Livemint.

Chase told customers during the outage that "some transactions are taking longer than usual to complete, but customers still have access to their accounts and funds," and stressed: "This is a technical issue, not a cybersecurity issue." At about 7 p.m. ET the bank told USA Today the issue had been resolved and was related to a "software bug"; by 7:25 p.m. ET it confirmed that "transactions are being processed normally now," as outage reports continued to fall.

Not a cyberattack, the banks and DHS say

Bank of America and U.S. Bank each said their own systems were not directly impacted; U.S. Bank said clients transacting with another institution through Zelle could see delays, and Bank of America said clients experiencing delays with other providers may wish to contact them directly. Zelle said its network was operating as it should and noted that it does not hold consumer funds - the participating banks do. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told Fox News on Monday night that DHS investigators do not believe the outages were caused by a cyberattack. Wells Fargo had not issued a statement quoted in the reports.

What to do if a payment is still missing

Chase says processing is back to normal, so a Zelle payment that was pending on Monday should complete without being re-sent - sending it again risks a duplicate once the original clears. If a payment still shows as delayed, the receiving bank is the one that can trace it: Bank of America's advice to its own customers was to contact the other provider involved in the transaction. Monday's outage was the third major US technology disruption in a week, after a global Microsoft Outlook and Teams outage and an FAA ground stop.
